notes.meaning: Paul and his fellow workers urge the believers not to treat God's gift of grace as an empty thing. Grace is God's free, undeserved favor in Christ that brings salvation. Believers should make sure that this wonderful message truly changes their lives.

differ.view: Believers truly receive grace by faith, but they receive it in vain if they do not continue in holiness.
This warning urges hearers of the gospel to bear genuine fruit so that outward preaching is not received without saving effect.

notes.meaning: Paul quotes Isaiah to show that God promised to hear and help His servant at the right time. That promised time has now arrived through the coming of Jesus Christ. Since salvation is offered right now, people should welcome it without delay.

Paul and his companions take great care not to put any stumbling block in front of others. They do not want anyone to turn away from the gospel because of bad conduct. Their goal is to protect the message of Christ from being discredited.

Instead of demanding praise, the apostles prove they are true servants of God by their actions. They show patient endurance when troubles, hardships, and severe pressures press in on them. Their willingness to suffer patiently commends their ministry to everyone watching.

Paul lists specific trials he faced, including beatings, jail time, and angry mob riots. He also experienced exhausting physical work, sleepless nights, and times without food. Through all these painful struggles, he remained faithful in serving Christ.

The apostles also proved their calling by how they lived inside and out. They showed moral purity, spiritual understanding, patience, and kindness to others. These good qualities were not human achievements, but gifts produced by the Holy Spirit and genuine love.

Paul preached the true message of the gospel with God's power backing it up. He carried weapons of righteousness in both hands, meaning God's truth protected him on every side like full armor. Righteous living was both his shield against attacks and his sword in spiritual battle.

The apostles served faithfully whether people praised them or despised them. Enemies called them deceivers and spread bad reports about them, yet they remained true and honest before God. They did not let human opinions steer them away from their mission.

The world treated the apostles as obscure nobodies, yet they were well known to God and to the church. They faced constant deadly dangers, but God kept them alive. Even when they were severely beaten and disciplined, God preserved their lives.

Outwardly, the apostles endured great grief, yet they always had inner joy in the Lord. They owned almost no earthly possessions, but they made many people rich by sharing the gospel. Though having nothing in this world, they truly possessed all things through Christ.

Paul addresses his readers warmly by name and tells them he has spoken with complete honesty. He hid nothing from them because his heart was wide open in love. His deep affection made his words flow freely and openly.

Paul explains that any distance between them did not come from his side. There was plenty of room in his heart for the Corinthians, but their own feelings toward him had grown cold and tight. They were holding back their affection because of suspicion or outside influence.

Paul speaks to them tenderly, as a loving father speaks to his own children. He asks for a fair return of the love he has poured out on them. He simply wants them to open their hearts wide to him as he has done for them.

Paul tells Christians not to harness themselves together with unbelievers in compromising partnerships. Just as oxen of different kinds cannot pull a plow together properly, God's people cannot share moral partnership with wickedness. Light and darkness belong to two opposite worlds and cannot mix.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view verses 14 through chapter 7 verse 1 as a separate fragment from another letter that was inserted here, while others see it as Paul's own sudden digression.

notes.meaning: Paul asks how Christ could ever be in harmony with Belial, an ancient name for Satan that means worthlessness. In the same way, someone who trusts in Christ has no common spiritual ground with an unbeliever. Their ultimate loyalties, hopes, and masters are totally opposed.

God's temple has no place for pagan idols, and Paul reminds the Corinthians that believers together are the living temple of God. Long ago God promised in Scripture that He would live with His people and walk among them. Because God makes His home among His people, their lives and worship must belong to Him alone.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Paul is drawing here on a collected list of Old Testament proof texts, joining several passages into one.

notes.meaning: Quoting the Old Testament prophet Isaiah, the Lord calls His people to step away from corrupt and idolatrous practices. They must keep themselves pure and avoid touching unclean things so they are not polluted by evil. When they separate themselves from worldly evil, God promises to welcome them with open arms.

The Lord Almighty promises to be a caring Father to all who belong to Him, receiving them as His own sons and daughters. This promise gives believers the highest honor and comfort possible. Since the all-powerful ruler of the universe is their Father, they can count on His complete protection and love.
